source_text:
Παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς, οὐκ ἐγώ, ἀλλ’ ἡ ἀγάπη Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ: μόνῃ τῇ χριστιανῇ τροφῇ χρῆσθε, ἀλλοτρίας δὲ βοτάνης ἀπέχεσθε, ἥτις ἐστὶν αἵρεσις:
οἳ ἑαυτοῖς παρεμπλέκουσιν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καταξιοπιστευόμενοι, ὥσπερ θανάσιμον φάρμακον διδόντες μετὰ οἰνομέλιτος, ὅπερ ὁ ἀγνοῶν ἡδέως λαμβάνει ἐν ἡδονῇ κακῇ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν.
thought_title: Only Christian food, not the poison of false teaching
orientation: Ignatius is warning the Trallians against false teachers who mix Christ with error, after saying he could not safely teach them heavenly things.
pass_a_gloss: I urge therefore you, not I, but the love of Jesus Christ: with only the Christian food use [yourselves], from foreign plant abstain, which is false teaching: [those] who with themselves weave in Jesus Christ, being trusted [as worthy], just as a deadly drug giving with honeyed wine, which the [one] not knowing sweetly takes in evil pleasure the to die.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the adjective and noun; 'Christian' is the standard English form of χριστιανός, and 'food' keeps the metaphor of nourishment that Ignatius contrasts with the poisonous herb.
ἀλλότριος means belonging to another, alien, foreign; βοτάνη is a plant or herb. 'Foreign herb' preserves the agricultural metaphor of something not belonging to the Christian field.

The compound combines καταξιόω (deem worthy) and πιστεύομαι (be trusted); the passive participle describes the false teachers presenting themselves as trustworthy while weaving Christ into their own schemes.
φάρμακον can mean medicine or poison; with θανάσιμον it is clearly a lethal substance. 'Deadly drug' keeps the ambiguity of a substance that appears beneficial but kills.
Literal rendering; the pleasure is qualified as evil, showing that the sweetness of the honeyed wine masks the death it brings.

pass_b_english: So I urge you, not I myself but the love of Jesus Christ: take only Christian food, and keep away from any foreign plant, which is false teaching.

These people weave Jesus Christ into themselves while claiming to be worthy of trust, like those who give a deadly poison mixed with honeyed wine. The one who does not know takes it gladly, with evil pleasure, and so receives death.

problems.quote: weave Jesus Christ into their own schemes
problems.why: They mix themselves with Jesus Christ, not weave him into their schemes.
problems.fix: mix Jesus Christ in with themselves
problems.ruling: ἑαυτοῖς is dative 'to themselves,' not 'their own schemes'; παρεμπλέκουσιν means 'mix/interweave themselves with' Christ.

problems.quote: presenting themselves as worthy of trust
problems.why: Means 'making him worthy of trust,' referring to Christ, not themselves.
problems.fix: making him out as worthy of trust
problems.ruling: καταξιοπιστευόμενοι is passive, referring to Christ being made trustworthy, not themselves presenting as trustworthy.

problems.quote: like someone giving a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine
problems.source_quote: ὥσπερ θανάσιμον φάρμακον διδόντες μετὰ οἰνομέλιτος
problems.why: Source has plural participle 'giving' matching 'οἳ' (these people), not 'someone giving'.
problems.fix: like those giving a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine
problems.ruling: διδόντες is plural, matching οἳ; 'someone' singular misrepresents the subject giving the drug.

edits.old: These people weave Jesus Christ into their own schemes, presenting themselves as worthy of trust, like someone giving a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine.
edits.new: These people mix Jesus Christ in with themselves, making him out as worthy of trust, like those giving a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine.

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says for 'weave Jesus Christ into their own schemes'? No, it was corrected.
The English already says exactly what the source says for 'presenting themselves as worthy of trust'? No, it was corrected.
The English already says exactly what the source says for 'like someone giving a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine'? No, it was corrected.

problems.quote: making him out as worthy of trust
problems.why: Misreads middle/passive participle: they make themselves worthy of trust/credibility, not Christ.

problems.quote: The one who does not know takes it sweetly, and in evil pleasure he takes death
problems.source_quote: ὅπερ ὁ ἀγνοῶν ἡδέως λαμβάνει ἐν ἡδονῇ κακῇ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν
problems.why: Misreads syntax: 'takes death' is object of λαμβάνει, not separate clause; 'sweetly' modifies taking, not separate action.
problems.fix: which the one who does not know takes sweetly with evil pleasure, taking death
problems.ruling: ὁ ἀγνοῶν ἡδέως λαμβάνει ἐν ἡδονῇ κακῇ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν: 'takes death' is object of λαμβάνει; current rendering splits into separate clauses, distorting syntax.

edits.old: making him out as worthy of trust
The one who does not know takes it sweetly, and in evil pleasure he takes death.
edits.new: The one who does not know takes it sweetly with evil pleasure, taking death.

problems.why: Middle voice means they trust themselves excessively, not appear trustworthy.
Infinitive articular expresses result/purpose: 'so as to die' or 'to their death'.
problems.ruling: τὸ ἀποθανεῖν is an articular infinitive of result/purpose: 'so as to die' or 'to their death,' not 'taking death.'

problems.why: Metaphor of poisonous plant/herb; 'foreign' may mislead as ethnic rather than 'alien to the faith'.

fixed: Changed 'foreign herb' to 'alien herb' to avoid the ethnic connotation of 'foreign' and better capture the sense of a plant alien to the faith.

problems.why: Mixed metaphor: 'herb' with 'food'; 'strange plant' or 'foreign vegetable'?
problems.fix: Check Greek; may be 'strange plant' or 'foreign drug' (pharmakon again).

problems.why: 'Herb' is likely 'plant' or 'weed' in a metaphor; 'alien herb' sounds like a drug reference.

fixed: Changed 'alien herb' to 'foreign plant' to avoid the drug connotation and better match βοτάνης as a plant metaphor.

problems.why: Multiple metaphors for heresy (myths, teaching, deceit, pleasure, plants, offshoots) may seem like different threats.
problems.fix: Add marginal note identifying these as varied metaphors for same danger.

problems.why: Abstract noun 'Christianity' appears twice; reader may not grasp this is rare early usage.
problems.fix: Note that 'Christianity' as abstract noun is unusual and significant.

problems.quote: deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine
problems.why: 'Drug' in modern English means medicine or narcotic; the context is poison.

edits.old: deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine
edits.new: deadly poison mixed with honeyed wine

fixed: The source θανάσιμον φάρμακον means a deadly poison, not a medicinal drug; 'poison' is the accurate rendering.
The source has no term for 'myths' or 'old myths'; the metaphors in the passage are all for false teaching (αἵρεσις), so no marginal note is needed.
The source uses Χριστιανισμός only once in this passage, not twice; no note is needed.

last_rejected.why: Misreads middle/passive: 'being trusted/trusting in their own worth' not 'trusting themselves beyond measure'.
last_rejected.fix: while they are credited with trustworthiness
last_rejected.ruling: καταξιοπιστευόμενοι middle = 'deeming themselves worthy of trust'; 'trusting themselves beyond measure' conveys this adequately.

last_rejected.why: Infinitive articular: 'with the result of dying' or 'unto death', but 'to their death' implies purpose/destination. 'The dying' or 'so as to die' better.
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ ἀποθανεῖν as articular infinitive expressing result; 'to their death' conveys outcome adequately.

last_rejected.quote: mix Jesus Christ in with themselves
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'they' (οἳ), object is Jesus Christ: 'they entwine Jesus Christ alongside themselves'—but English 'mix in with themselves' obscures that they weave JC into their own system.
last_rejected.fix: they weave Jesus Christ in alongside themselves
last_rejected.ruling: παρεμπλέκουσιν = interweave/mix in; 'mix Jesus Christ in with themselves' captures the sense adequately.

polish.changed: Clarified the metaphor and pronoun references, made the speakers and objects explicit, and smoothed the sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Mixed metaphor: 'herb' with 'food'; 'strange plant' or 'foreign vegetable'?
notes.fix: Check Greek; may be 'strange plant' or 'foreign drug' (pharmakon again).

notes.why: 'Herb' is likely 'plant' or 'weed' in a metaphor; 'alien herb' sounds like a drug reference.

polish.changed: Clarified that the poisoners are the false teachers, kept the metaphor of foreign plant and Christian food intact, and rendered the poison image as 'deadly poison mixed with honeyed wine' to avoid the modern ambiguity of 'drug.'

notes.why: Multiple metaphors for heresy (myths, teaching, deceit, pleasure, plants, offshoots) may seem like different threats.
notes.fix: Add marginal note identifying these as varied metaphors for same danger.

notes.fix: Note that 'Christianity' as abstract noun is unusual and significant.
